title: Reducing Pre-Normalization Centered-Advantage Variance Through Counterfactual Reasoning Paths
claim: Transforming within-group weights before aggregation cancels shared-token gradients, whereas untransformed asymmetric aggregation leaves residual gradient and drift.
layout: Single wide panel, left-to-right flow, with dashed inset branching to symmetric path
description: A wide, rounded dashed-border panel showing a left-to-right pipeline. An input prompt feeds an LLM backbone, drawn as stacked transformer blocks with FFN and attention, in blue and lavender. The backbone produces several sets of green 3D-block responses, τ1 through τt. These go to a blue Reward & Advantage Calculate box. From there, advantages and importance ratios branch into two paths. The upper path goes to a pink-gray Asymmetric Aggregation box. It has a scale icon, Σ≠0, and a distribution plot showing drift. The lower path goes through a dashed green Within-Group Transformation box. It contains Option 1 Min-Replace and Option 2 Orth-Proj, and feeds a Symmetric Aggregation box with Σ=0 and a stable distribution plot. Both paths merge into a blue Parameter Update box at the right. Math notation appears throughout, and arrows carry labels such as Â_i, W_i and R_ℓ.
caption: Overview of the DFPO pipeline. After sampling multiple responses for the same input, the method computes group-relative advantages and sequence-coupled importance weights, forming the effective token modulation W. It then applies a within-group transformation, Min-Replace or Orth-Proj, to remove within-group asymmetry in W, so that shared-token gradients cancel under symmetric aggregation (P = 0). This reduces the learning tax and stabilizes parameter updates. The upper-right comparison illustrates how asymmetric aggregation without the transformation leads to gradient non-cancellation (P̸ = 0) and probability drift.
abstract: Reinforcement learning for multi-step reasoning with large language models (LLMs) typically relies on sparse terminal rewards, which can create a poorly conditioned credit-assignment problem: the final feedback is propagated uniformly across all intermediate decisions. This can lead to high gradient variance, unstable training, and many ineffective updates, potentially limiting sustained model improvement. We propose a counterfactual-comparison framework for credit assignment. For each input, the framework samples multiple reasoning trajectories and treats their differences as implicit approximations to alternative decisions. This yields an implicit process-level advantage estimator that converts sparse terminal rewards into step-sensitive learning signals. Building on this framework, we introduce Implicit Behavior Policy Optimization (IBPO), which improves performance on mathematical and code-reasoning benchmarks. Our results point to a promising direction for unlocking the reasoning potential of LLMs.
